q: An email from 'IT Support' says your account will be disabled and asks you to verify your password at a link. You should:
opts: Click the link and log in quickly
Verify through the official app or call IT on a known number
Reply to the email with your password
Forward it to a colleague to check
exp: Never authenticate from an email link. Verify via the official app or a number you already trust.

q: You find a USB drive labelled 'Payroll 2026' in the parking lot. You should:
opts: Hand it to security without plugging it in
Plug it into a work machine to scan it
Plug it into your personal laptop to see whose it is
Keep it; finders keepers
exp: Dropped media is a classic baiting vector (and modern sticks can emulate a keyboard). Hand it in untouched.

q: A caller claims to be the helpdesk and asks you to read out the MFA code that just arrived. You should:
opts: Read out the code so they can fix it
Give the caller your password to speed things up
Hang up and call the helpdesk on the published number
Press 1 to speak to a supervisor
exp: No legitimate helpdesk needs your MFA code or password. Hang up and call back on a number you trust.

q: A text says a parcel is held and you must pay a $1.99 fee via a link. You should:
opts: Tap the link and pay the small fee
Reply STOP to unsubscribe
Forward the text to friends to warn them
Open the official carrier/retailer app and check your order
exp: Small unexpected fees are the pretext to harvest full card data. Never act on a delivery link; check the real app.

q: The CEO emails you to send an urgent wire transfer and says to keep it confidential. You should:
opts: Process the wire immediately to keep it secret
Verify by calling the executive on a known number and follow the finance process
Reply to the email to confirm the details
Ask the sender for their bank details
exp: Business email compromise relies on secrecy and urgency to bypass process. Verify out of band; never skip controls.

q: Your phone is flooded with MFA push prompts you did not request. You should:
opts: Approve the push so the prompts stop
Ignore it and change nothing
Deny the request and report it to security
Share the code in the work chat so IT can investigate
exp: MFA fatigue (push bombing) means someone has your password and is trying to get you to approve. Deny and report.

q: Which practice best defends against credential stuffing (reusing leaked passwords)?
opts: Reuse one strong password everywhere so you never forget it
Write passwords in a shared team document
Use your pet's name plus the year
Use a password manager with unique passwords and enable MFA
exp: Unique passwords stop one breach from unlocking other accounts, and MFA blunts a stolen password.

q: A caller says they are from your bank's fraud team and asks for the one-time code to release your card. You should:
opts: Give the one-time code so they can release the card
Hang up and call the number printed on your card
Give your card number and CVV to verify
Provide your online banking password
exp: Banks never ask for OTPs, CVV, or passwords. A 'code we sent' request is the account-takeover pattern.

q: Someone without a badge follows you through the secure door carrying boxes. You should:
opts: Politely ask them to badge in and report anyone without a badge
Hold the door - it's rude not to
Let them in if their hands are full
Assume they work there and move on
exp: Tailgating bypasses every technical control. Challenge politely and report; you will never be penalized for it.

q: A colleague emails an unexpected 'Benefits' spreadsheet with a prompt to 'Enable Content' to view it. You should:
opts: Enable macros so you can see the content
Open it and see what happens
Verify the sender out of band and never enable macros from email attachments
Disable your antivirus first so it opens
exp: Macro-enabled documents are a top malware delivery vector. Confirm the sender on another channel; don't enable content.

q: A login page looks identical to your company SSO and shows a padlock. What is the reliable check?
opts: Enter your credentials since the page looks identical
Check the URL and reach the site by typing the known address
Trust it because it has a padlock
Test it with your work email and password
exp: Look-alike pages and TLS certificates are easy to fake. Read the domain and navigate to the site yourself.

q: How can your own social media usage help a spear-phishing attacker?
opts: It can't; social media is separate from work
Only if you post your password
Public role, projects, travel, and relationships feed targeted pretexts - so limit public details
It only matters for celebrities
exp: Public details become the personal hooks in spear-phishing. Tighten privacy settings and share less publicly.

q: While browsing, a site shows a pop-up: 'Your Flash/plugin is outdated - download the update now.' You should:
opts: Close it and update only through the official OS/app updater
Install the update from the pop-up
Download the installer from the pop-up link
Ignore all updates forever
exp: Fake update pop-ups deliver drive-by payloads. Patch only through built-in updaters or trusted vendor channels.

q: An unexpected email asks you to scan a QR code to 'renew your password'. You should:
opts: Scan the QR to reach the portal quickly
Scan it but don't enter the password
Share the QR with IT so they can scan it
Never scan QR codes from email; navigate to the official site directly
exp: QR codes hide their destination from hover/preview checks. Go to the official portal by typing the address yourself.
